items.prompt: What's the key difference between a unit test and an integration test?
choices: Unit tests are always shorter files than integration tests
A unit test checks one function/module in isolation; an integration test checks that multiple REAL components actually work together correctly (real contracts, not mocks)
There's no real difference — the terms are interchangeable
Integration tests can only be written in certain programming languages
items.explanation: Isolation is the defining property of a unit test — dependencies are typically mocked or absent. Integration tests specifically exercise real components together, which is what lets them catch contract mismatches a unit test's mocks would hide.

items.prompt: Why does the test pyramid recommend MANY unit tests, FEWER integration tests, and the FEWEST e2e tests, rather than an equal number at each level?
choices: Because unit tests are considered more important than the other two levels

Because the shape reflects a real cost/confidence/specificity trade-off — unit tests are cheapest to write, run, and diagnose, while e2e tests are the most expensive per test, so the highest layer is reserved for the smallest number of critical, whole-flow checks
Because most testing frameworks technically only support a limited number of e2e tests
The shape is arbitrary convention with no underlying reasoning
items.explanation: L2 frames this explicitly as a cost trade-off: e2e tests are slowest, most fragile, and least specific on failure — reserving them for a small number of critical flows, while relying on the cheaper unit level for the bulk of coverage, is what keeps the overall suite fast and diagnosable.

items.prompt: A team has mostly e2e tests and very few unit tests (the "inverted pyramid"). Per L2, is this necessarily MORE thorough than a well-shaped pyramid with equivalent coverage?
choices: Yes — more e2e tests always means more thorough testing

No — it inherits e2e's costs at scale (slow suite, hard-to-diagnose failures, high flakiness) without necessarily catching more real bugs than an equivalent, well-shaped pyramid; it just costs more to run and trust
Yes, because e2e tests are inherently more reliable than unit tests
No, because inverted pyramids are technically impossible to implement
items.explanation: L2 is explicit: the inverted shape doesn't necessarily catch more bugs — it pays e2e's cost (speed, fragility, diagnostic difficulty) for coverage that could often be achieved more cheaply and reliably at a lower level.

items.prompt: A test labeled "integration test" mocks out the discount service entirely and only checks that the frontend calls a function with the right arguments. Per L3's failure modes, what's the problem?
choices: Nothing — mocking is always appropriate for integration tests

It's a unit test wearing an integration test's name — since nothing real is actually being contacted, it can't catch a real contract mismatch between the frontend and the actual service, which is the entire point of testing at the integration level
The problem is that it doesn't run fast enough
The problem is that it should be an e2e test instead
items.explanation: L3 explicitly warns against this: heavy mocking in a nominally-integration test defeats its purpose, since integration tests exist specifically to verify real components' contracts actually match — a mock just returns whatever shape was assumed when it was written, which is exactly the assumption a real integration test is meant to check.

items.prompt: An e2e test fails intermittently. Per L3's failure modes, should this be treated with the same confidence as a failing unit test (i.e., assume it's a real regression)?
choices: Yes — any test failure should always be treated as a confirmed regression

No — e2e tests have the highest fragility of the three levels (most moving parts: network, timing, rendering), so an intermittent failure needs actual triage to distinguish a real regression from an environment/timing flake, unlike a unit test which almost never fails for unrelated reasons
No, because e2e test failures should always be ignored
Yes, but only if the test has failed more than three times in a row
items.explanation: L2's fragility comparison and L3's failure modes both point to this directly: e2e's dependence on the most moving parts makes intermittent failures common for reasons unrelated to the actual code, which is exactly why they warrant investigation before being trusted as strongly as a unit test failure.

items.prompt: Implement `classifyTestLevel({ isPureLogic, touchesRealComponent, drivesRealBrowser })`, encoding L2's decision procedure: if `drivesRealBrowser` is true, return "e2e". Otherwise, if `touchesRealComponent` is true, return "integration". Otherwise (pure, isolated logic), return "unit".

tests.description: pure logic with no real dependencies is a unit test
tests.expr: expect(classifyTestLevel({ isPureLogic: true, touchesRealComponent: false, drivesRealBrowser: false })).toBe('unit')

tests.description: touching a real component (real DB/service) is an integration test
tests.expr: expect(classifyTestLevel({ isPureLogic: false, touchesRealComponent: true, drivesRealBrowser: false })).toBe('integration')

tests.description: driving a real browser is an e2e test, even if it also touches real components
tests.expr: expect(classifyTestLevel({ isPureLogic: false, touchesRealComponent: true, drivesRealBrowser: true })).toBe('e2e')

items.explanation: This mirrors L2's decision flowchart exactly: the most expensive/broadest condition (a real browser driving the whole flow) takes precedence, since an e2e test by definition also exercises real component integration along the way — the level is determined by the widest scope of what's actually being verified, not just any single property in isolation.
